review.limitations: The later metalogic, completeness and computability developments were not reviewed. Schröder–Bernstein is stated without proof in this introductory passage; this guide does not supply or certify that proof.

evidence.description: Comparison of sizes and limits of enumerations

sections.title: What this book provides
sections.text: A foundations text leading toward the study of logic itself. Its opening set-theory material supplies a shared language for collections, relations, functions and infinite sizes. These selected pages are useful independently of the later technical logic.

sections.title: Key distinctions
sections.text: Symmetric and antisymmetric are not opposites: equality satisfies both. Equivalence requires reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity and produces classes of related elements. A surjection reaches its entire declared codomain; an injection never sends distinct inputs to the same output.

sections.title: How the text reasons
sections.text: Precise quantified definitions are followed by tests on examples. The identity, successor and constant maps on natural numbers separate function properties. Cardinal comparison is then recast using maps, making statements about infinite sizes meaningful without finishing a count.

sections.title: Conclusions in the selected material
sections.text: A bijection expresses equal cardinality. Injections each way imply one exists by Schröder–Bernstein, which the introductory section asks readers to accept without proof. Diagonal arguments defeat supposed exhaustive lists by constructing a missing object.

sections.title: What to take into an experiment
sections.text: State the underlying set whenever you define a relation, and check each required property separately. For a transformation, distinguish its allowed inputs, allowed outputs and reached outputs. These habits clarify when a collection of transformations really acts on a set.
